title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40)
hookLine: speak to the heart of Jerusalem; they that hope in the Lord shall run and not be weary

cards: Handel's Messiah begins, after the overture, with a single tenor voice, almost alone, singing two words, and then singing them again: Comfort ye. Handel set the King James wording.
But the words were written for people who needed them far more than a concert crowd. Five days ago on this path, Jerusalem burned and its people were marched to Babylon.
Isaiah chapter forty sounds like a voice reaching those exiles, after years of silence by foreign rivers. And God's very first word to them is not a scolding.

teach.b: In the King James: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." The Douay-Rheims: "Be comforted, be comforted, my people." Said twice, the way you'd say it to a crying child.

teach.h: SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.
teach.b: Then, in the Douay: "Speak ye to the heart of Jerusalem." Some readers hear in that Hebrew phrase a way of saying speak tenderly, the way someone speaks to win back a person they love. Her time of punishment is over.

teach.h: PREPARE THE WAY OF THE LORD.
teach.b: Then a voice cries out: prepare the way of the Lord in the desert, make a straight road. Every valley lifted up, every mountain made low.
All four Gospels apply that voice to John the Baptist, getting the road ready for Jesus. Then a sobering line: all flesh is grass, and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever.
And the chapter ends with God, who never grows tired, giving strength to the weary. Young people stumble and fall.
"But they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall take wings as eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint."
Notice the order: soar, run, walk.

teach.h: THEY SHALL RUN AND NOT BE WEARY.
teach.b: Not every day is a flying day. Sometimes the promise is simply to keep walking. Some scholars call these later chapters Second Isaiah and set them in the exile; the Church receives the whole book as Isaiah's, read as one.
Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after their fast for the fallen Temple, and call that Sabbath Nachamu, comfort.

how: Catholics hear Isaiah 40 in Advent, including the Second Sunday of Advent in one year of the cycle, and the voice crying in the wilderness is heard as John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ.

o: God's tender first words to his exiled people
a line Handel wrote for a London concert crowd
a prophet's warning that punishment is coming

games.q: comfort for the exiles — tap the pairs.
p: said twice, like to a crying child
is grass, and the flower fades

s: God's first words in Isaiah 40 are a rebuke
they're comfort, twice, and the news that Jerusalem's sin is forgiven.
all four Gospels apply the voice in the desert to John the Baptist
prepare ye the way of the Lord.
the eagles line promises only soaring
it moves from soaring to running to walking without fainting.

games.q: you're the prophet, sent to people who've lost their city and their Temple, and who know they brought some of it on themselves. how do you begin?
o: with a list of what they did wrong.
with comfort, and the news their sin is forgiven.
with a plan to rebuild the walls.
games.why: comfort ye, comfort ye my people. speak to the heart of Jerusalem: her time of punishment is over, her iniquity forgiven.

practice: Think of someone in a long exile of their own: grief that hasn't lifted, a diagnosis, loneliness, a job search going nowhere.
Instead of a speech, find one tender, simple sentence that speaks to their heart: it's not over, and you're not forgotten. If you pray, ask God to comfort them, twice, the way Isaiah says it.

wordCard.voice: Comfort ye. God's first words to his exiled people in Isaiah forty, said twice, tenderly: the end of punishment and the start of the road home. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: comfort ye, the chapter's first word. It gives its name to Shabbat Nachamu in the Jewish year.

carryVoice: Your line: comfort, my people. Said twice, and said to the heart. See you tomorrow.
